g.data-qualified-name: THE WAIT-WORD CONTRACT - why a bounded read cannot answer inside the request.why4
g.text: R1 answers in the request's own CRC
cycle, so it carries ZERO wait words
and an unchanged R1 host needs no change.
The response BYTES are unchanged; wait
THE RESPONSE BIT IS WHAT MAKES THE TWO
DIRECTIONS ASYMMETRIC ON THE WIRE. A host
request never has opcode bit 7 set, so a
response is distinguishable from a request by
that bit alone: 0x01 PING asks, 0x81 PING
answers. A request with bit 7 already set is
not a request at all - it answers
LENGTH COUNTS WORDS, AND "len must be 0"
IS A REAL CONSTRAINT, NOT A CONVENTION.
all take len 0; DEBUG_BP_SET takes exactly
one word (the breakpoint address). The wrong
length is a BAD_FRAME, so a rejected op has
no side effect - which is what makes S5
THE 16-SLOT BUFFER IS WHERE THE 15 COMES FROM.
R2 grew the response buffer from 8 to 16 slots
to hold the 11-word header, and the slot count
is the ceiling on a single read: 16 slots minus
the status word is 15 data words (30 bytes for
READ_DMEM). A larger count is answered RANGE so
the host splits the transfer - it is never
THE RULE IS SCOPED TO THE BOUNDED READS. 0x13
READ_IMEM and 0x14 READ_DMEM are the ops that
must fetch, and they are the only ops that emit
filler. READ_CPU (0x12) and all four debug ops
request's own CRC cycle, so they emit ZERO
filler words. A host must therefore tolerate
fillers without assuming every op has them.
A filler word cannot be a header, so the host's
skip never has to guess: it stops at the first
word that could be a header, and everything after
that is validated normally. The bad-CRC case is
answered BAD_FRAME, which is a header too - so a
corrupt frame is still found, not skipped past.
Frame sync - fixed, opens both directions
Control - opcode, target, sequence, length, status
Integrity - the CRC word, always last
Transport - wait words and the rules around them
